141.title: The head
141.hook: the head box sits above the forehead, where thought begins
141.howItsDone: After the arm box, the head box is placed above the hairline, centered, with its knot at the back of the head and the straps hanging forward over the shoulders; many say a second blessing over it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shel yad: the arm box, angled toward the heart. Your line was hand and heart together. Today, the second box.

The verse says "between thine eyes." Yet look at someone wearing tefillin and you won't find a box on the bridge of the nose. You'll find it higher, up at the hairline, above the middle of the face. That's the part of a person that frowns when they're worried, that gets rubbed when they're thinking hard, that a palm presses against after a mistake. It's where thinking seems to happen. And that's where the second box goes.
screen: `BETWEEN THINE EYES?` → `NO: UP AT THE HAIRLINE.` → `WHERE THINKING SEEMS TO HAPPEN.`

segments.voice: It's called the shel rosh, the one of the head. The verse says the words shall be "for frontlets between thine eyes," and the rabbis, reading it with other verses, placed the box above the hairline, centered over the space between the eyes, where a baby's soft spot is. The strap circles the head and is tied in a knot at the back, at the top of the neck, and the two ends hang down in front, over the shoulders. Why the head? The arm box binds the heart and the hand, what you want and what you do. But a third thing needs binding: what you think. Thoughts wander. They race at three in the morning. The head box says that even your thinking can be pointed somewhere. Look closely and you'll see a Hebrew letter pressed into the leather on its sides: shin. The knot at the back is shaped like the letter dalet, and the small knot by the arm box like a yud. Together, shin, dalet, yud spell Shaddai, one of the names of God. Then comes a daring passage. The Talmud asks: does God wear tefillin? And it answers yes. What's written inside God's tefillin? Ours hold a verse praising God. God's hold a verse from Chronicles praising the people Israel, asking who is like them, one nation on earth. It's a picture of love going both ways. The people bind God's words to their heads; God, so to speak, binds theirs.

segments.voice: Put your fingers at your hairline and notice what your mind has been circling today. Choose where you'd like it to go instead, in a few words, be kind, or pay attention, or don't rush, and press your fingers lightly, as if tying the thought in place. When the mind wanders, bring it back.
The head. The head box of tefillin, bound above the hairline, so that thoughts, too, are tied to something higher.
Your line: thoughts get bound too. The arm holds the heart; the head holds the thought. Day one hundred forty-one, done.

142.title: Winding the strap (Hosea 2:21–22)
142.hook: wrapping the finger, many say "And I will betroth thee unto Me for ever"
142.howItsDone: After the head box, the arm strap is wound around the middle finger and hand; many Jews say Hosea 2:21–22 as they wrap the finger three times. Winding customs differ between Ashkenazi, Sephardi and Hasidic communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the head box, above the hairline, and God's own tefillin. Your line was thoughts get bound too. Today, the last step of putting them on.

A wedding ring is a small thing, a thin band of metal. Yet some people touch theirs all day without noticing, turn it when they're nervous, miss it for weeks if they take it off. It's not what it's made of. It's what it says: I'm bound to someone, and they're bound to me. Now, the last moment of putting on tefillin. Both boxes are on. The long strap from the arm still hangs free. The person takes it and, slowly, wraps it around one finger. Three times. Like a ring.
screen: `A THIN BAND OF METAL.` → `WHAT IT SAYS: BOUND.` → `THREE TIMES AROUND ONE FINGER.`

segments.voice: After the head box is on, the rest of the arm strap is wound around the hand: three times around the middle finger, then across the palm, often tracing the shape of the letter shin, for Shaddai, the name from yesterday. The customs differ: Ashkenazi, Sephardi and Hasidic Jews wind in different directions and patterns, each handed down from parents and teachers. As they wrap the finger, many say two verses from the prophet Hosea. In Hosea, God speaks to the people like a spouse after a long, painful separation, promising to start again: "And I will betroth thee unto Me for ever; yea, I will betroth thee unto Me in righteousness, and in justice, and in lovingkindness, and in compassion. And I will betroth thee unto Me in faithfulness; and thou shalt know the LORD." Betroth is engagement language. From the same Hebrew root comes erusin, the first stage of a Jewish marriage. So the last act of putting on tefillin is a kind of daily wedding: the strap around the finger like a ring, and the words of a promise. Look at what's promised: righteousness, justice, lovingkindness, compassion, faithfulness. Not a list of feelings, but of how two parties treat each other. And Hosea's words come after a story of betrayal and hurt. The promise isn't made by people who've never failed each other. It's made by people starting again. Every weekday morning, before the main prayers, the people who say these verses renew it.

Your line: like a ring. A small band can carry a big promise. That's day one hundred forty-two.

143.title: Who wears them
143.hook: traditionally men from bar mitzvah; in many non-Orthodox communities women wear them too
143.howItsDone: In Orthodox communities, men and boys from bar mitzvah wear tefillin each weekday morning. In many Conservative and liberal communities, women may wear them too, and in Reform communities wearing them is a personal choice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, erusin: three turns around the finger, like a ring, with Hosea's promise. Your line was like a ring. Today, the last day on tefillin, and a real question.

Two synagogues on the same street, the same weekday morning. In the first, the men's section is full of arms wrapped in black straps, fathers next to sons, a boy of twelve putting them on for the first time while his grandfather watches. The women pray on their own side, without tefillin. In the second, a woman in her forties winds a strap around her arm, next to a teenage girl doing the same. Both rooms pray the same prayers. Each follows a reading it has thought through. And both are Jewish.
screen: `TWO SYNAGOGUES, ONE STREET.` → `A BOY AND HIS GRANDFATHER.` → `A WOMAN WINDING A STRAP.`

segments.voice: Traditional Jewish law says men are obligated to wear tefillin from bar mitzvah, which the Mishnah puts at thirteen, the age of commandments. In some communities, boys start practicing a little before. Women, in traditional law, are exempt. Not forbidden: exempt, under a general rule that women are exempt from positive commandments tied to a set time, and tefillin are worn by day. Then comes a surprising line in the Talmud: Michal, the daughter of King Saul, wore tefillin, and the sages did not protest. Rabbis argued for centuries over what to make of that. Some said a woman may choose to take on the practice; later codes, like the Rema's notes to the Shulchan Aruch, discouraged it. Today each community answers with its own reasons. Orthodox communities generally keep the traditional practice: men wear tefillin, women don't. Conservative Judaism teaches that women may take on the commandment, and its law committee has ruled they can be equally obligated, so in many Conservative synagogues, women wear tefillin. In Reform and other liberal communities, tefillin are a personal choice for anyone; some people of all genders wear them, and many don't wear them at all. Some Jews wear them only now and then, and outreach volunteers on city streets offer to help a passing Jewish man put them on for a minute. All of these communities care about the same verse and the same boxes. They differ over who is bound by it. Learning that a custom isn't yours is not the same as thinking it's wrong.

144.title: What kosher means
144.hook: kosher means fit; some Jews keep the food laws fully, some partly, some not at all
144.howItsDone: Jews who keep kosher eat only permitted foods, prepared and supervised according to Jewish law, often checking for a kosher symbol on packaged food. Observance ranges from full kashrut at home and away to partial or none.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tefillin, and how each community answers who wears them. Your line was customs differ, respect holds. Keep it close: today we open the Jewish food laws.

You've probably said it yourself. Is that kosher? Meaning: is that allowed, is that legit? It's one of the Hebrew words that made it all the way into everyday English. Then there's the other place you've seen it: a little symbol on a box of crackers, a sign in a deli window. Most people have a rough idea. No pork. Something about meat and milk. A rabbi blessing the food, maybe? That last one isn't it. So what does kosher actually mean?
screen: `IS THAT KOSHER?` → `A SYMBOL ON THE CRACKERS.` → `WHAT DOES IT ACTUALLY MEAN?`

segments.voice: Kosher, kasher in Hebrew, means fit, proper, right for its purpose. It appears in the book of Esther, when the queen asks the king for a favor, "and the thing seem right before the king." Right, fit: kasher. It isn't only about food. A Torah scroll can be kosher, fit for reading. So can a shofar, or a sukkah. The system of food laws is called kashrut, fitness. And no, a rabbi's blessing doesn't make food kosher. What it is and how it was prepared does. Over the next few days: which animals the Torah permits, meat and milk, care for animals, and why people keep it. The Torah gives the basic outline; rabbinic law built it out in detail. Kosher food also needs supervision. That's what the symbols on packages mean: an agency has checked the ingredients and the process. Here's the part that surprises people. Not all Jews keep kosher, and those who do don't all keep it the same way. Some keep it fully, at home and away. Some keep a kosher home but eat more freely outside. Some avoid pork and shellfish and leave it there. Some don't keep it at all, and some keep an ethical version, focused on how food is raised. In America, surveys suggest a minority of Jews keep kosher at home. That's not a scorecard. It's a people making choices about something they take seriously. What almost everyone shares is the idea underneath: eating is never just eating. It's a choice, three times a day.

segments.voice: Think of the last thing you ate: where it came from, who made it, whether you chose it or it just happened. No judgment, just noticing. Then picture choosing your next meal on purpose, for any reason that matters to you: health, kindness, tradition, gratitude.
Kosher. Fit, proper: food prepared according to Jewish law, and a word for anything right for its purpose.

145.title: Which animals (Leviticus 11)
145.hook: land animals that chew the cud and have split hooves, fish with fins and scales
145.howItsDone: Jews who keep kosher eat mammals with split hooves that chew the cud, fish with fins and scales, and birds with a tradition of being eaten, and check packaged foods for a kosher supervision symbol.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kosher: fit, proper, and kept in many ways. Your line was eating is a choice. Today, the first question of the food laws: which animals.

A puzzle. Cow: yes. Sheep: yes. Goat, deer: yes. Pig: no. Camel: no. Rabbit: no. Salmon: yes. Tuna: yes. Shrimp: no. Lobster: no. Catfish: no. What's the rule? A common guess: animals that are dirty, or dangerous to eat. That's not what the Torah says. The rule is almost a biology test, written out in one chapter of Leviticus, and it's surprisingly simple. Two signs for land animals, two for fish.
screen: `COW YES, PIG NO.` → `SALMON YES, SHRIMP NO.` → `WHAT'S THE RULE?`

segments.voice: For land animals, Leviticus eleven says: "Whatsoever parteth the hoof, and is wholly cloven-footed, and cheweth the cud, among the beasts, that may ye eat." Two signs: split hooves, and chewing the cud, bringing food back up to chew it again, like cows, sheep, goats and deer. It needs both. The Torah names the famous exceptions. The camel chews the cud, but its hoof isn't split the way the verse requires. The pig has split hooves but doesn't chew the cud. One sign each, so neither is eaten. In the water: "whatsoever hath fins and scales" may be eaten. Salmon and tuna, yes. Shellfish, with neither, no. Catfish, no scales, no. Birds get no signs, just a list of those not eaten, which in English translations includes vultures, ravens, hawks and owls. The old Hebrew names are hard to identify now, so Jews who keep kosher eat only birds with a long tradition of being eaten, like chicken, duck and turkey. Insects are nearly all forbidden, though the Torah permits certain locusts, and some Yemenite Jews still keep a tradition of which ones. Now, why? The Torah doesn't say. It never mentions health. Maimonides suggested health reasons; others, like Abarbanel, disagreed, and some say the point is that the Torah simply doesn't explain. What it does say is: be holy. The rules create a daily pause, a difference between what's chosen and what's passed over. And since packaged food can hide ingredients, people who keep kosher read labels closely and look for a symbol from a supervising agency.

146.title: Meat and milk (Exodus 23:19)
146.hook: "thou shalt not seethe a kid in its mother's milk" grew into separate dishes and waiting times
146.howItsDone: Jews who keep kosher don't cook or eat meat (including poultry) with dairy, keep separate dishes and utensils for each, and wait between meat and dairy according to family custom, often one, three or six hours.

segments.voice: Yesterday, which animals: split hooves and chewing the cud, fins and scales. Your line was read the label.

Open the cabinets in a home that keeps kosher, and you might think they own twice the dishes they need. Two sets of plates, two sets of pots, two sets of silverware, sometimes with colored handles, red for one, blue for the other. Sometimes two sinks. Ask someone there if they want ice cream after a burger, and they might check the clock first. It all grows out of one short sentence in the Torah. A sentence about a baby goat.
screen: `TWO SETS OF DISHES.` → `RED HANDLES, BLUE HANDLES.` → `CHECKING THE CLOCK.`

segments.voice: "Thou shalt not seethe a kid in its mother's milk." Seethe means boil; a kid is a young goat. It's an oddly specific rule, and the Torah gives it not once but three times, twice in Exodus and once in Deuteronomy. The rabbis took that repetition seriously: three mentions, three prohibitions. Don't cook meat and milk together, don't eat them together, and don't benefit from the mixture, like selling it. Then they widened it, from a goat and its own mother's milk to any meat and any dairy. By rabbinic law, poultry counts as meat too. Fish and eggs are neither; they're called pareve, neutral, and can go with either. Pots and pans can absorb flavors, so kitchens keep separate dishes. And after eating meat, Jews who keep kosher wait before eating dairy. How long depends on family custom: some wait six hours, some three, some one, each handed down in different communities. All are respected traditions. Why this rule at all? The Torah doesn't say. Some commentators suggested it was to keep away from an ancient pagan practice. Others heard compassion in it: the milk meant to give a young animal life shouldn't be used to cook it. One puzzle the rabbis noticed: when Abraham hosts three visitors in Genesis, he serves them curd, milk and a calf, all at once. Different sages gave different answers to how that fits. They didn't hide the question.

segments.voice: Picture your plate, empty, at the moment you'd reach for a second helping, and notice what the wanting feels like, right in the body. Then just wait. Not to punish yourself, but to see the space between one thing and the next.
Pareve, neutral foods like fish and eggs that count as neither meat nor dairy, and can be eaten with either under the kosher rule of meat and milk.
Your line: some things stay apart. Even in one kitchen. Day one hundred forty-six, done.

147.title: Care for animals
147.hook: Jewish law forbids causing animals needless suffering
147.howItsDone: Jewish law forbids causing animals needless suffering; many Jews feed their animals before eating themselves, let working animals rest on Shabbat, and expect kosher slaughter to be a single swift cut.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pareve: neither meat nor milk, and a kitchen with two sides. Your line was some things stay apart. Today, the animals themselves.

A calf is being led to slaughter. It breaks away, runs to Rabbi Judah the Prince, the sage tradition credits with compiling the Mishnah, hides its head in his clothes, and cries. The rabbi says to it: go. This is what you were created for. The Talmud says that because he showed no pity, he suffered years of illness. Then one day his housekeeper was sweeping out some baby weasels, and he stopped her.
screen: `A CALF RUNS TO THE RABBI.` → `GO, THIS IS WHAT YOU'RE FOR.` → `THEN, THE BABY WEASELS.`

segments.voice: He told her to leave them alone, quoting a psalm: "His tender mercies are over all His works." Because he showed mercy, the Talmud says, his suffering ended. That story sits at the heart of a principle in Jewish law called tza'ar ba'alei chayim, the suffering of living creatures: you may not cause an animal needless pain. The Talmud debates whether the rule comes straight from the Torah or from the rabbis, and later authorities argue both ways. Look how many of the Torah's laws protect animals. If you see even your enemy's donkey collapsed under its load: "thou shalt surely release it with him." Help him, enemy or not, for the animal's sake. "Thou shalt not muzzle the ox when he treadeth out the corn": let a working animal eat from what it's working on. On Shabbat, your ox and donkey rest too. If you take eggs from a nest, first send the mother bird away. The Talmud even draws a mealtime rule from a verse in the Shema, which says God will give grass for your cattle, and then says you'll eat and be satisfied. Cattle first, then you. So Jewish law says to feed your animals before you sit down to eat. It connects back to kosher food too: the traditional method of slaughter, shechita, is meant to be a single swift cut, and an animal that's badly injured or diseased isn't kosher. Look back at the week: the head, the strap like a ring, who wears them, what kosher means, which animals, meat and milk, and now the animals' own suffering.
screen: `OVER ALL HIS WORKS.` · `NO NEEDLESS SUFFERING.` · `RELEASE THE DONKEY, EVEN AN ENEMY'S.` · `FEED YOUR ANIMALS FIRST.` · then, large: `HIS TENDER MERCIES ARE OVER ALL.`

segments.voice: Picture an animal near you, a pet, a bird at the window, an insect you'd usually swat, a dog on the sidewalk, and notice it has a body like yours: it gets hungry, tired, scared. Then choose one small kindness you could offer it: fresh water, a gentle hand, or simply letting it go out the window instead of squashing it.
Ba'alei chayim. Living creatures, the Hebrew phrase at the heart of the Jewish principle that you may not cause an animal needless pain.
Your line: animals feel too. Mercy for a calf, a weasel, an enemy's donkey. Until tomorrow.
